title: The Price of Attention
focus: Discourse markers in lectures (by way of illustration, turning to, in other words)

lines.text: Good morning. I want to start with a remark made by the economist Herbert Simon, who observed that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention.
That was written long before smartphones, which is rather remarkable. By way of illustration, think about what happens when you pick up your phone to check the time.
You intend to spend five seconds. Twenty minutes later, you're reading about something you had no interest in at breakfast.
Turning to why this happens, it's tempting to blame our own weakness. To put it differently, we assume that the failure is personal.
I'd like to suggest that this is only half the story. Many of these products are designed by teams whose success is measured by how long people stay.
Take the infinite scroll. There's no natural stopping point, which means the decision to stop has to come from you, every single time.
Similarly, automatic playback removes a pause that used to exist between one episode and the next. That pause was where you might have asked yourself whether you actually wanted another.
Some designers compare the unpredictable rewards of a feed to a slot machine. The analogy isn't perfect, but it captures the idea that not knowing what comes next is itself compelling.
Now, I don't want to sound alarmist. Most of these tools are useful, and in some respects the picture is more nuanced than the headlines suggest.
For instance, people who use social media to keep in touch with friends tend to report better wellbeing than those who simply scroll. In other words, what you do matters more than how long you do it.
Having said that, it would be naive to put the entire burden on users. As a result, some countries are considering rules that would limit certain design features for young people.
Whether such rules would work remains to be seen. On the one hand, they might protect the vulnerable; on the other, they could prove difficult to enforce.
Let me conclude, then, by returning to Simon. If attention is the scarce resource, we ought to treat it as we treat any other: as something worth defending.
For the seminar, please keep a log of your phone use for three days, and note the moments when you wished you'd stopped sooner.

options: He sees it as a complete explanation
He sees it as a dishonest explanation
He sees it as an outdated explanation
He sees it as a partial explanation
questions.explain_es: Actitud. 'I'd like to suggest that this is only half the story.'

options: Programmes have become noticeably shorter
Prices have risen for most services

Design has removed a natural chance to stop
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. 'Removes a pause that used to exist... where you might have asked yourself whether you actually wanted another.'

questions.q: Why does he mention the slot machine comparison?
options: To prove that all users are addicted
To illustrate why unpredictability holds attention
To claim that feeds are illegal gambling
To show that designers are dishonest
questions.explain_es: Propósito. 'Not knowing what comes next is itself compelling.' Además aclara que la analogía 'isn't perfect'.

questions.q: What does he say about people who use social media to keep in touch with friends?
options: They tend to spend less time online
They tend to suffer more anxiety
They tend to report better wellbeing

questions.explain_es: 'Tend to report better wellbeing than those who simply scroll.'

questions.explain_es: 'The decision to stop has to come from you, every single time.'

questions.explain_es: Dice que 'some countries are considering rules'; aún no están en vigor.

dictation: Whether such rules would work remains to be seen.
If attention is the scarce resource, we ought to treat it as we treat any other.

title: Letting Go of the Boxes
focus: Past habits with would and used to

lines.text: This week, minimalism, a word that I used to roll my eyes at.
You did, Kate. You would always tease me about my empty shelves.
I would. I used to think it was a pose, something that people with large, quiet flats could afford.
And now you've given away half your wardrobe.
A third, let's say. What changed was a house move. I used to keep boxes I'd never opened, and I would tell myself that I might need the contents one day.
That's the classic reasoning. Might need it is the sentence that fills every attic.
Exactly. And when I finally opened those boxes, I'd forgotten what was in most of them. That told me something.
It tells most people something. But I'd warn against making it into a religion. I knew someone who would throw away a book the moment she had finished it.
That sounds rather joyless.
To me it did, until she explained that she'd grown up in a house where nothing could ever be thrown away.
Ah. So her minimalism was a reaction.
In a way. Which suggests that the real aim isn't owning less, it's being free from the compulsion in either direction.
I like that. I'd say my own aim is simpler: I'd like to spend less time looking for things.
A modest but sensible ambition. Does it help with money, too?
A bit. I used to buy things to cheer myself up, and I'd feel worse by the evening. I buy far less now.
Then maybe minimalism is less about stuff than about noticing why you want it.
That's a good place to stop. Thanks, Ben.

Fearful, seeing it as a risk
questions.explain_es: Actitud. 'I used to think it was a pose.'

questions.explain_es: 'The real aim isn't owning less, it's being free from the compulsion in either direction.'

title: Justice for Those Who Can't Pay
focus: Formal collocations (prohibitive costs, a common thread, of limited value)

lines.text: You run a free legal advice centre in a busy town. What kind of problems do people bring you?
Mostly housing and debt, followed by employment disputes. The common thread is that people come to us when matters have already reached a crisis.
Why so late?
Partly pride, partly fear. Many people assume that seeking advice is an admission that they've done something wrong, which is rarely the case.
Is it true that most people can't afford a lawyer?
For a dispute that goes to court, yes, the costs can be prohibitive. A single hearing can cost more than someone earns in a month.
So justice depends on your income?
In practice, to a degree it does, and I won't pretend otherwise. In principle, everyone is equal before the law, but equal rights are of limited value if you can't afford to enforce them.
That's a strong statement.
It's an observation, not an accusation. Plenty of lawyers give their time free, and that makes a real difference, though it can't fill the gap.
What would you change if you could?
I'd put more money into early advice. A letter written in week one can resolve what would otherwise become a case lasting a year.
That sounds more efficient than court.
It is, and it saves public money in the long run, although the saving is hard to see because it doesn't appear in any one budget.
Do you ever worry that you're treating symptoms?
Every day. But the person in front of me has a notice on the door, not a policy debate. I'd be failing them if I waited for the system to change.

To show the value of early advice
questions.explain_es: Propósito. 'A letter written in week one can resolve what would otherwise become a case lasting a year.'

title: When the Ice Runs Out
focus: Speculating about the future (is likely to, is set to, could well)

lines.text: Welcome. Our subject is the tropical glaciers of the Andes, and what their retreat means for the cities that drink from them. Doctor Salinas, where do we stand?
Frankly, in a difficult place. These glaciers are shrinking, and they're likely to keep shrinking whatever we do over the next few decades.
From the perspective of a farmer, the question is less about ice and more about water in the dry season. And that's when glaciers matter most.
Precisely. They act like a bank account. They store water in the wet months and release it slowly when the rain stops.
And the account is being drained?
For now the opposite is true, which is the trap. More ice melts, so rivers carry more water, and everybody feels reassured. Eventually, though, the flow is set to fall sharply.
That's what worries us. If planning is based on today's river levels, we could well build for a future that won't exist.
What would better planning look like?
Storing water in the wet season, repairing leaking channels, and choosing crops that need less. None of it is glamorous, but it's cheap compared to a crisis.
I'd add that the most vulnerable cities are probably those that have grown fastest, because their demand has risen while their supply is about to shrink.
Is there a danger of overstating it? Glaciers aren't the only source of water, after all.
A fair challenge. Rain, groundwater and wetlands all contribute, and in some valleys they matter more. The picture will vary enormously from place to place.
That's true, and it's one reason why national plans are no use unless they listen to local communities.
So no single answer?
No, though one point is firm: we'd be wise to act before the river drops, not after.
Agreed. Waiting would be the costliest choice of all.

questions.explain_es: Actitud. 'They're likely to keep shrinking whatever we do.'

title: Two Hotels, One Payroll
focus: Conditional inversion (should you…, were we to…, had it not been for…)

lines.text: Thank you for meeting us. As you know, the merger will go ahead, and we'd like to discuss how it affects staff.
Of course. If you have any concerns about job security, I'd like to address them straight away.
We do have concerns. Were the two hotels to share one reception team, many people would lose their posts.
I won't deny there will be some overlap. Had it not been for the merger, we would probably have closed one site altogether, which would have been far worse.
That may be so, but it isn't much comfort to those affected. Should redundancies prove unavoidable, what will you offer?
If we did have to reduce staffing, we would offer retraining first and redundancy only as a last resort.
Retraining for what, though? Had the company already identified new roles, you'd have said so.
That's a fair point. Not yet, but we'd expect new positions in the combined events department, should the plan go ahead as intended.
I'd want that in writing. If those roles fail to materialise, people will feel they've been misled.
I can put a commitment in writing, with one caveat: it can't be a guarantee, since much depends on bookings.
A commitment with a caveat is better than nothing, I suppose. Now, on pay. Were staff to move between sites, would travel costs be covered?
Within reason, yes. Had we not budgeted for it, we would risk losing many of our best people.
Then that's a point in your favour. I'd like to take the draft to our members before we agree to anything.
Naturally. If they raise questions, we're willing to meet again.
Then let's reconvene on Thursday.
Thursday it is.

title: Major Revisions
focus: Contrastive linking (whilst, whereas, in contrast, nevertheless, albeit)

lines.text: I've finished the review of the soil study. Whilst the dataset is impressive, I have some concerns about the conclusions.
Go on. I found it persuasive, whereas you seem less convinced.
In the first part, the authors compare treated and untreated plots, which is reasonable. In contrast, the second half compares different farms, and that's where it falls apart.
Because the farms differ in other ways, you mean.
Exactly. Soil type, rainfall, even who manages the land. Nevertheless, the authors write as if the difference were due to the treatment alone.
That is a leap. Although I'd say they hedge it in the discussion.
They do, albeit in a single sentence, whereas the abstract states the finding as fact. And the abstract is what most people read.
True. So we'd ask for a rewrite of the abstract. What about the statistics?
Whilst the methods are sound, one figure doesn't match the table. It may be a typo, but I'd want it checked.
Agreed. On the other hand, I wouldn't reject on that basis. It seems fixable.
Neither would I. My recommendation is major revisions rather than rejection, since the work is valuable even though the claims go too far.
I'd go the same way, though I'd be a little more generous in tone. These authors are early in their careers.
Fair. We can be firm about the science and still be kind. In contrast to some reviewers I've met, I do try.
I know. Send me your draft and I'll merge them.

title: Bringing a Language Back
focus: Nominal clauses (what matters is that…, the fact that…, whether…)

lines.text: Good afternoon. Today's question is whether a language that has almost fallen silent can be brought back, and what it takes to do so.
It's often assumed that a language dies because people stop speaking it. What's closer to the truth is that people stop passing it on to their children.
That distinction matters, because it tells us where to intervene. Whether a language survives depends largely on what happens in the home.

Take Hebrew, which had been used for prayer and writing for centuries but was not an everyday spoken language. It was brought back into daily speech, and today millions use it as their first language.
That is an unusual case, and I wouldn't want you to think that it's a model. The fact that it succeeded owes a great deal to particular political circumstances.
A more typical example is Welsh. What helped there was that the language had a place in schools, in broadcasting and in public life, and not only at home.
Similarly, Māori communities in New Zealand set up pre-schools known as language nests, in which very young children are immersed in the language by older speakers.
The idea that elders are a resource, rather than a relic, is central to this approach. What these programmes do is link grandparents to grandchildren.
Now, what many people overlook is that revival is not simply a question of teaching. It's whether the young people feel that the language belongs to them.
If speaking it feels like a school exercise, they'll drop it. If it feels like a way of belonging, they might use it with friends.
That's why music, comedy and social media matter so much. What a school can't supply is the sense that the language is alive and slightly rebellious.
I should add a note of caution. Revived languages often change; the speakers of the new generation don't talk exactly like their grandparents.
Some purists find that troubling. My own view is that a language which never changes is a language which is no longer spoken.
So what counts as success? It depends on who you ask, but I'd say that success is when a child chooses the language without being told to.
For next week, please read the two case studies and decide which factors you consider most transferable.

title: Rules for the Food Stall
focus: Comparative correlatives and degree adverbs (the more…, considerably, marginally)

lines.text: Tonight: should street food vendors face stricter regulation? Mr Ortiz, you represent about two hundred vendors.
I do, and the more rules we add, the fewer people can afford to trade. Most vendors earn very little, and each new licence is a cost they have to carry.
I understand that, but a handful of badly run stalls can affect a great many customers. The more people a stall serves, the more important basic hygiene becomes.
Nobody disagrees with hygiene. But the inspections we see are often arbitrary. A vendor can be fined on one day for something that's overlooked on another.
That's an argument for clearer standards, not fewer inspections. Considerably more consistency would benefit everyone.
Mr Ortiz, would clearer standards satisfy you?
Largely, yes. Provided they're affordable, and provided vendors have time to adapt. A rule that arrives on Monday and applies on Tuesday is no help.
I'd accept a transition period. It would be marginally slower, but I'd rather it work than be resented.
Doctor Pearce, how serious is the health risk, honestly?

It's often exaggerated, and I'll say so. The vast majority of stalls cause no problems at all. But when something goes wrong, the consequences can be severe, particularly for children and the elderly.
And let's remember that street food is also how a great many ordinary people eat safely and cheaply every day.
Granted. The more we treat vendors as partners, the better the outcomes tend to be. Training schemes often work better than fines.
That I can support. We'd gladly organise it ourselves, as long as the city provides the water and facilities.
So there's more common ground than expected.
Considerably more. The disagreement is about how, not whether.
I'd put it slightly differently. It's about who pays.
A fair note to end on. Thanks to you both.

title: The Payments That Didn't Add Up
focus: Narrative tenses (past perfect simple and continuous)

lines.text: Martin, you were an accountant at a mid-sized construction firm. What had you noticed before you decided to speak up?
I'd been working on the accounts for nearly two years when I realised that certain payments had been recorded under the wrong headings. At first I'd assumed it was carelessness.
When did that change?
When I found out that the same payments had been going through for months. Somebody had been doing it deliberately, and I'd been signing off the reports without noticing.
That must have been a shock.
It was. I hadn't slept properly for weeks, because I'd been going over it in my head. I kept asking whether I was misreading things.
Did you talk to anyone?
My wife, first. She'd been telling me for a while that something was bothering me. Then my manager, who told me, very politely, that I should drop it.
What did that tell you?
That he'd probably known all along. Nobody had threatened me, but the message was clear.
And so you went outside the company.
Eventually. I'd spent a month collecting copies of documents, which I'd been advised to do, and then I contacted the regulator.
How did the company react?
Within weeks I'd been moved to a role with no responsibilities. By then I'd stopped expecting thanks.
Looking back, would you do it again?
Yes, though I'd prepare better. I hadn't understood how lonely it would be.
Thank you for being so candid.
Thank you for listening.
